pos: a. (covered with cloud; almost always in the Authorized Version of the cloudy pillar in which the LORD led and spoke to Israel)
etymology: From cloud — Old English clud, a rock or hill, transferred to a cumulus mass — with -y. The Hebrew at Exodus 33:9 is ammud he-anan, the pillar of the cloud; at Ezekiel 30:3 the word is anan alone, of a day heavy with judgment.
biblical_def: Five of the six occurrences of cloudy concern one object: the pillar in which the LORD went before Israel. “And it came to pass, as Moses entered into the tabernacle, the cloudy pillar descended, and stood at the door of the tabernacle, and the LORD talked with Moses” (Exodus 33:9). The people did not see a form; they saw a cloud, and they worshipped — “all the people saw the cloudy pillar stand at the tabernacle door: and all the people rose up and worshipped” (Exodus 33:10). Nehemiah recalls the same in his great prayer of national confession: “thou leddest them in the day by a cloudy pillar; and in the night by a pillar of fire, to give them light in the way wherein they should go” (Nehemiah 9:12). The Psalmist adds that it was the medium of speech as well as of guidance: “He spake unto them in the cloudy pillar: they kept his testimonies, and the ordinance that he gave them” (Psalm 99:7). The cloud is thus both revelation and concealment — God truly present and truly hidden, which is exactly the condition of a holy God dwelling among a sinful people. Ezekiel takes the other sense: “the day of the LORD is near, a cloudy day; it shall be the time of the heathen” (Ezekiel 30:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines cloudy as overcast with clouds, and figuratively as obscure, dark, or gloomy of aspect.
webster_full: CLOUDY, a. Overcast with clouds; obscured with clouds; as a cloudy day; a cloudy sky; a cloudy night.
2. Consisting of a cloud or clouds; as a cloudy pillar. Ex. 33.
3. Obscure; dark; not easily understood.
4. Having the appearance of gloom; indicating gloom, anxiety, sullenness, or ill nature.
CLOUD, n. A collection of visible vapor, or watery particles, suspended in the atmosphere at some altitude.
scriptures: Exodus 33:9
And it came to pass, as Moses entered into the tabernacle, the cloudy pillar descended, and stood at the door of the tabernacle, and the LORD talked with Moses.
Exodus 33:10
And all the people saw the cloudy pillar stand at the tabernacle door: and all the people rose up and worshipped, every man in his tent door.
Nehemiah 9:12
Moreover thou leddest them in the day by a cloudy pillar; and in the night by a pillar of fire, to give them light in the way wherein they should go.
Psalm 99:7
He spake unto them in the cloudy pillar: they kept his testimonies, and the ordinance that he gave them.
corruption_summary: The pillar is reduced to a natural phenomenon or a later legend, and the doctrine it teaches — God present and hidden at once — is lost with it.
corruption_paragraphs: Critical treatments of the exodus narratives regularly explain the cloudy pillar as a volcanic plume, a caravan brazier, or a theological figure composed centuries after the event to dignify a national origin story. Each explanation must dispose of the same feature: the cloud spoke, and it moved according to a purpose, and it stood at the tabernacle door when Moses entered and not otherwise. Neither a volcano nor a brazier does that. The dictionary takes the narrative as it stands, written by Moses, of an event Israel witnessed together and Nehemiah recited a thousand years later as fact in a prayer of confession.

The theological loss is greater than the historical one. The cloud teaches something no other image teaches so well: that God draws near and remains hidden in the drawing near. The people saw the pillar, not a form; they were led truly and shown nothing. That is the condition of all revelation before the incarnation, and it explains why John writes that the Word was made flesh and dwelt — tabernacled — among us, and we beheld his glory. What Israel saw as cloud, the disciples saw as a Man. The cloudy pillar is not superseded by that; it is fulfilled in it, and it returns at the transfiguration and at the ascension.
roots_summary: Hebrew anan, a cloud — Exodus 33:9, Ezekiel 30:3; ammud, a pillar or column — Nehemiah 9:12; shekinah is the later rabbinic term for the indwelling glory.
roots_lines: Hebrew anan — a cloud; the standard word for the pillar, Exodus 33:9 and Psalm 99:7.
Hebrew ammud — a pillar or column; joined to anan for the guiding pillar.
Hebrew araphel — thick darkness; the companion term at Sinai, Exodus 20:21.
Hebrew kabod — glory, weight; what the cloud both contained and concealed.
Ezekiel 30:3 uses the same root for a day of judgment — a cloudy day, the time of the heathen.
usage: “The cloudy pillar descended, and stood at the door” — presence and concealment together.
“He spake unto them in the cloudy pillar” — the cloud was a medium of speech, not only of guidance.
“A cloudy day; it shall be the time of the heathen” — the other sense, of judgment.

pos: a. (tempestuous; four times of the stormy wind — twice as an obedient servant of God's word, twice as the instrument of His fury)
etymology: From storm — Old English storm, a tumult — with -y. The Hebrew at Psalm 107:25 is ruach searah, a wind of tempest; searah is the whirlwind out of which the LORD answered Job.
biblical_def: Every occurrence in the Authorized Version joins the adjective to one noun: the stormy wind. And every one of them makes the wind a servant. “For he commandeth, and raiseth the stormy wind, which lifteth up the waves thereof” (Psalm 107:25) — the great psalm of those who go down to the sea in ships, where the storm is not an interruption of God's government but an exercise of it, raised at command and stilled at command. The hallelujah psalm enrolls it in the choir: “Fire, and hail; snow, and vapour; stormy wind fulfilling his word” (Psalm 148:8). The phrase is decisive for the doctrine of providence: the wind does not merely happen, it fulfils his word. Ezekiel turns the same wind against a false ministry. The prophets had daubed a flimsy wall with untempered morter, and the LORD says: “there shall be an overflowing shower; and ye, O great hailstones, shall fall; and a stormy wind shall rend it” (Ezekiel 13:11), and again, “I will even rend it with a stormy wind in my fury” (Ezekiel 13:13). What comfort is to the sailor who cries unto the LORD is destruction to the man who has been whitewashing a wall that will not stand.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines stormy as tempestuous, agitated with furious winds, and figuratively as violent or passionate.
webster_full: STORMY, a. Tempestuous; agitated with furious winds; boisterous; as a stormy season; a stormy day or night.
2. Proceeding from violent winds; as stormy gusts.
3. Violent; passionate.
STORM, n. A violent wind; a tempest.
2. A violent assault on a fortified place; a furious attempt of soldiers to enter and take a fortified place by scaling the walls.
scriptures: Psalm 107:25
For he commandeth, and raiseth the stormy wind, which lifteth up the waves thereof.
Psalm 148:8
Fire, and hail; snow, and vapour; stormy wind fulfilling his word:
Ezekiel 13:11
Say unto them which daub it with untempered morter, that it shall fall: there shall be an overflowing shower; and ye, O great hailstones, shall fall; and a stormy wind shall rend it.
Ezekiel 13:13
Therefore thus saith the Lord GOD; I will even rend it with a stormy wind in my fury; and there shall be an overflowing shower in mine anger, and great hailstones in my fury to consume it.
corruption_summary: Weather is assigned to a closed system of secondary causes, and the biblical claim that the storm fulfils God's word is treated as poetry.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern instinct is that a storm is fully explained when its meteorology is described, and that any further claim is decoration. Scripture does not deny secondary causes — Psalm 148 lists fire, hail, snow, and vapour as the ordinary furniture of the sky — but it refuses to stop there. He commandeth, and raiseth the stormy wind. Stormy wind fulfilling his word. The Reformed doctrine of providence holds both: God governs all things by means, and the means are genuinely operative, and He is no less the governor for using them. A universe of pure mechanism has no room for Psalm 107; a universe of bare miracle has no room for meteorology; the confession holds the two together.

The pastoral consequence is what makes the doctrine worth contending for. If the storm is only weather, then the sailors' cry in Psalm 107 is addressed to nobody who can act, and the calm that follows is coincidence. If the wind fulfils His word, then the men at their wits' end are crying to the One who raised it, and He maketh the storm a calm. Ezekiel supplies the sobering half. The same wind that answers a sailor's prayer rends the whitewashed wall of the false prophets, and a ministry built with untempered morter will meet the weather eventually.
roots_summary: Hebrew searah, a tempest or whirlwind — Psalm 107:25, 148:8; ruach, wind or spirit — the noun it qualifies; saar, to sweep away — Ezekiel 13:11.
roots_lines: Hebrew searah — a tempest, whirlwind; the wind out of which the LORD answered Job, Job 38:1.
Hebrew ruach — wind, breath, spirit; the noun qualified in every occurrence of stormy.
Hebrew saar — to sweep away as with a storm; Ezekiel 13:11 and 13:13.
Hebrew tsavah — to command; Psalm 107:25, “he commandeth, and raiseth.”
Psalm 148:8 makes the wind an obedient servant: “stormy wind fulfilling his word.”
usage: “He commandeth, and raiseth the stormy wind” — the tempest under orders.
“Stormy wind fulfilling his word” — the whole doctrine of providence in four words.
“A stormy wind shall rend it” — the same wind against a whitewashed wall.

pos: n. pl. (peals of thunder; the sound at Sinai, and the recurring accompaniment of the throne and the opened temple in the Revelation)
etymology: From thunder — Old English thunor, cognate with the Norse god-name — with the plural verbal noun ending. The Hebrew at Exodus 20:18 is qolot, literally voices; the Greek at Revelation 4:5 is brontai, thunders.
biblical_def: The Hebrew for thunderings at Sinai is simply voices, and the ambiguity is not accidental. “And all the people saw the thunderings, and the lightnings, and the noise of the trumpet, and the mountain smoking: and when the people saw it, they removed, and stood afar off” (Exodus 20:18). They had just heard the ten words spoken; what accompanied the speaking was itself a kind of speech, and the effect was terror and distance — they stood afar off and asked that God speak to them through Moses. The Revelation takes up the same sound and attaches it to the throne: “And out of the throne proceeded lightnings and thunderings and voices” (Revelation 4:5). It recurs at each opening of a new phase. When the angel casts the censer of prayers to the earth, “there were voices, and thunderings, and lightnings, and an earthquake” (Revelation 8:5). When the temple of God is opened in heaven and the ark of His testament seen, the same list appears with hail added (Revelation 11:19). John is deliberately writing Sinai into his vision: the God who thundered on the mountain is the God on the throne, and the ark of the covenant given there is seen at last in heaven.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines thunder as the sound which follows an explosion of electricity in the atmosphere, and notes its scriptural use of God's voice and terrible power.
webster_full: THUNDER, n. The sound which follows an explosion of electricity or lightning; the report of a discharge of electrical fluid.
2. Thunder is used to express any loud tumultuous noise.
3. In Scripture, thunder is employed as an emblem of God's power.
The thunder of his power who can understand? Job 26.
THUNDERING, ppr. Making a loud noise as thunder; publishing with a loud voice.
scriptures: Exodus 20:18
And all the people saw the thunderings, and the lightnings, and the noise of the trumpet, and the mountain smoking: and when the people saw it, they removed, and stood afar off.
Revelation 4:5
And out of the throne proceeded lightnings and thunderings and voices: and there were seven lamps of fire burning before the throne, which are the seven Spirits of God.
Revelation 8:5
And the angel took the censer, and filled it with fire of the altar, and cast it into the earth: and there were voices, and thunderings, and lightnings, and an earthquake.
Revelation 11:19
And the temple of God was opened in heaven, and there was seen in his temple the ark of his testament: and there were lightnings, and voices, and thunderings, and an earthquake, and great hail.
corruption_summary: The fear of God is treated as a primitive stage religion has outgrown, so that Sinai is read as a stage effect rather than a revelation of what God is.
corruption_paragraphs: A widespread account of biblical religion holds that it evolved from a fearful tribal deity of storm and mountain toward a benign God of love, and that Exodus 20:18 belongs to the discarded stage. The Revelation defeats the scheme by placing the thunderings at the throne in the last book of the canon, and by opening the heavenly temple to display the very ark of the testament given at Sinai. The same voice sounds at both ends of Scripture. Hebrews, having urged that we are not come unto the mount that burned with fire, closes the chapter with our God is a consuming fire — the contrast is in the access, not in the God.

The pastoral effect of losing the thunderings is that worship becomes casual and grace becomes cheap. Israel stood afar off and were right to; what they lacked was a mediator, and God gave them one in figure and later in fact. A church that has forgotten the mountain will not marvel at the boldness with which it enters the holiest by the blood of Jesus, because it never understood what stood in the way. The right recovery is not to reintroduce terror but to preach the mediator — and no man preaches him greatly who has not first heard the thunder.
roots_summary: Hebrew qolot, voices — Exodus 20:18; Greek brontai, thunders — Revelation 4:5, 8:5, 11:19; phonai, voices — the companion term in John's triad.
roots_lines: Hebrew qol (plural qolot) — a voice or sound; rendered thunderings at Exodus 20:18.
Greek bronte — thunder; the plural at Revelation 4:5 and twice more in the visions.
Greek phone — a voice; joined to the thunders in each of John's lists.
Greek astrape — lightning; the third member of the recurring triad.
The Hebrew ambiguity is doctrinal: what accompanied God's speaking was itself called voices.
usage: “All the people saw the thunderings” — the Hebrew says voices.
“Out of the throne proceeded lightnings and thunderings and voices” — Sinai at the throne.
“There was seen in his temple the ark of his testament” — the covenant of Sinai, opened in heaven.

pos: v. (past participle of blow; in the Authorized Version chiefly of the trumpet sounded in war, in worship, and at the great ingathering)
etymology: From Old English blawan, to blow. The Hebrew at Amos 3:6 is taqa, to thrust or drive, and so to blow a trumpet by driving breath through it; at Isaiah 27:13 the noun is shophar, the ram's-horn trumpet.
biblical_def: A trumpet blown in an Israelite city was never a neutral sound. Amos makes the point with two rhetorical questions that carry his whole doctrine of providence: “Shall a trumpet be blown in the city, and the people not be afraid? shall there be evil in a city, and the LORD hath not done it?” (Amos 3:6). The first question is obvious — of course the alarm frightens them — and it is set there to make the second unavoidable. Ezekiel shows the alarm sounded to an army that will not come: “They have blown the trumpet, even to make all ready; but none goeth to the battle: for my wrath is upon all the multitude thereof” (Ezekiel 7:14). Nothing is wrong with the trumpet; the paralysis is judicial. Isaiah gives the great and hopeful use: “in that day, that the great trumpet shall be blown, and they shall come which were ready to perish in the land of Assyria, and the outcasts in the land of Egypt, and shall worship the LORD in the holy mount at Jerusalem” (Isaiah 27:13). The trumpet that gathers the perishing and the outcast is the one the New Testament takes up at the last trump. Job supplies a stranger use: “a fire not blown shall consume him” (Job 20:26) — a fire no man kindled and no bellows fed.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) gives blown as the participle of blow, and defines the sounding of a wind instrument by forcing breath through it.
webster_full: BLOWN, pp. Driven by wind; fanned; sounded by blowing.
BLOW, v.t. To throw or drive a current of air upon; to fan.
2. To sound a wind instrument; as, blow the trumpet.
3. To drive by a current of air; to impel.
TRUMPET, n. A wind instrument of music, used chiefly in war and military exercises.
scriptures: Amos 3:6
Shall a trumpet be blown in the city, and the people not be afraid? shall there be evil in a city, and the LORD hath not done it?
Isaiah 27:13

And it shall come to pass in that day, that the great trumpet shall be blown, and they shall come which were ready to perish in the land of Assyria, and the outcasts in the land of Egypt, and shall worship the LORD in the holy mount at Jerusalem.
Ezekiel 7:14
They have blown the trumpet, even to make all ready; but none goeth to the battle: for my wrath is upon all the multitude thereof.
All darkness shall be hid in his secret places: a fire not blown shall consume him; it shall go ill with him that is left in his tabernacle.
corruption_summary: Amos 3:6 is softened until God is no longer the author of calamity, which is precisely the claim the prophet is making.
corruption_paragraphs: Amos 3:6 is among the most avoided verses in the English Bible, and the avoidance takes several forms — that evil here means only calamity and therefore the verse says less than it appears to; that the LORD merely permits rather than does; that the prophet is speaking loosely. The first observation is correct and does not help: the Hebrew ra is indeed calamity rather than moral wickedness, and the question is precisely whether God is the author of calamity. Amos says He is. Isaiah says the same in the first person: I make peace, and create evil: I the LORD do all these things. The 1689 Confession holds the line without making God the author of sin, distinguishing His holy decree from the sinful means creatures freely employ — a distinction the Scripture itself makes when Joseph tells his brothers that they thought evil and God meant it unto good.

The reason the doctrine matters is that the alternative is worse. A God who does not govern calamity is a God who cannot answer prayer about it, cannot promise that all things work together for good, and cannot be trusted in the dark. Amos's rhetorical structure is the pastor's ally, not his enemy: the alarm is sounded so that the city may fear and repent, and the God who raised the trouble is the God who may be sought. Isaiah 27:13 is where the trumpet finally leads — the perishing and the outcast gathered to worship in the holy mount.
roots_summary: Hebrew taqa, to thrust, to blow a trumpet — Amos 3:6, Ezekiel 7:14; shophar, the ram's horn — Isaiah 27:13; nephach, to blow or fan — Job 20:26.
roots_lines: Hebrew taqa — to drive or thrust, and so to blow a horn; Amos 3:6 and Ezekiel 7:14.
Hebrew shophar — the ram's-horn trumpet; Isaiah 27:13, “the great trumpet.”
Hebrew chatsotserah — the silver trumpet of the priests; Numbers 10:2, the other instrument.
Hebrew nephach — to breathe or fan; Job 20:26, of a fire no man kindled.
Hebrew ra — evil in the sense of calamity; the disputed word at Amos 3:6.
usage: “Shall a trumpet be blown… and the people not be afraid?” — the obvious question set before the hard one.
“They have blown the trumpet… but none goeth to the battle” — a judicial paralysis.
“The great trumpet shall be blown” — the perishing and the outcast gathered.

pos: a. and v. (moistened; in Daniel, of the king wet with the dew of heaven through seven years of beast-madness, and in Job of the poor without shelter)
etymology: Old English waet, moist, cognate with water. The Aramaic of Daniel is tseba, to dip or moisten — the same root as the verb used of dipping in dye; the recurring phrase is tal shemayya, the dew of heaven.
biblical_def: Five of the six occurrences belong to a single sentence of judgment, repeated four times as decree, warning, fulfilment, and later testimony. The watcher's decree: “let it be wet with the dew of heaven, and let his portion be with the beasts in the grass of the earth” (Daniel 4:15). Daniel's warning to the king: “they shall wet thee with the dew of heaven, and seven times shall pass over thee, till thou know that the most High ruleth in the kingdom of men, and giveth it to whomsoever he will” (Daniel 4:25). The fulfilment: “his body was wet with the dew of heaven, till his hairs were grown like eagles' feathers, and his nails like birds' claws” (Daniel 4:33). And Daniel's reminder to Belshazzar a generation later (Daniel 5:21). The repetition is the point — the purpose clause is stated before the judgment falls, so the reader knows it is corrective and not merely punitive. Nebuchadnezzar wet with dew is a king reduced to the condition of the grass he grazed on, and the end of it is a doxology from his own mouth. Job uses the word of the destitute: “They are wet with the showers of the mountains, and embrace the rock for want of a shelter” (Job 24:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines wet as containing water or other liquid, moist, humid — and as a verb, to fill or moisten with liquid.
webster_full: WET, a. Containing water, as wet land; or having water or other liquid upon the surface, as a wet table.
2. Rainy; as wet weather; a wet season.
WET, n. Water or wetness; moisture or humidity in considerable degree.
WET, v.t. To fill or moisten with water or other liquid; to sprinkle; to dip in liquor and withdraw.
DEW, n. The water or moisture collected or deposited on or near the surface of the earth in the night.
scriptures: Daniel 4:25

That they shall drive thee from men, and thy dwelling shall be with the beasts of the field, and they shall make thee to eat grass as oxen, and they shall wet thee with the dew of heaven, and seven times shall pass over thee, till thou know that the most High ruleth in the kingdom of men, and giveth it to whomsoever he will.
Daniel 4:33

The same hour was the thing fulfilled upon Nebuchadnezzar: and he was driven from men, and did eat grass as oxen, and his body was wet with the dew of heaven, till his hairs were grown like eagles' feathers, and his nails like birds' claws.
Daniel 4:37
Now I Nebuchadnezzar praise and extol and honour the King of heaven, all whose works are truth, and his ways judgment: and those that walk in pride he is able to abase.
Job 24:8
They are wet with the showers of the mountains, and embrace the rock for want of a shelter.
corruption_summary: Nebuchadnezzar's madness is filed under psychiatry and the doctrine drained out of it — that God abases the proud and restores whom He will.
corruption_paragraphs: Daniel 4 is regularly handled as a case study, with the king's condition given a clinical name and the narrative treated as a legend built around an illness. The text is not shy about the physical facts — the hair, the nails, the grass, the dew — but it refuses to let them be the explanation. The purpose is stated three times before the event and once after: till thou know that the most High ruleth in the kingdom of men, and giveth it to whomsoever he will. That is not a diagnosis; it is a verdict, and it was published in advance so that the king would recognise it when it came.

The doctrine at stake is the abasement of the proud and the sovereignty of God over kingdoms, and Nebuchadnezzar himself states it in the closing doxology: those that walk in pride he is able to abase. He walked upon his palace and said Is not this great Babylon, that I have built; while the word was in his mouth the sentence fell; and after seven times his understanding returned and he blessed the most High. Reformed readers have always taken this chapter as the plainest scriptural picture of God humbling a man in order to save him, and of a conversion effected by a providence no counsellor would have prescribed. Job 24:8 keeps the other end in view: the same dew and rain fall on the poor who have no shelter, and God sees them too.
roots_summary: Aramaic tseba, to moisten or dip — Daniel 4:15, 25, 33; tal, dew — the recurring phrase; Hebrew ratab, to be moist — Job 24:8.
roots_lines: Aramaic tseba — to dip, to moisten; the verb in every Daniel occurrence.
Aramaic tal shemayya — the dew of heaven; the phrase repeated four times in the judgment.
Aramaic illaya — the most High; the title used throughout the chapter, and the point of the whole judgment.
Hebrew ratab — to be moist, wet; Job 24:8 of the destitute in the mountains.
Old English waet — moist; cognate with water.
usage: “They shall wet thee with the dew of heaven” — the sentence announced before it fell.
“Till thou know that the most High ruleth” — the stated purpose of the madness.
“Those that walk in pride he is able to abase” — the king's own conclusion.

pos: a. (muddy, boggy; of the pit from which David was drawn, the marshes left unhealed, and the clay in the feet of Nebuchadnezzar's image)
etymology: From mire — Old Norse myrr, a bog — with -y. The Hebrew at Psalm 40:2 is tit ha-yaven, clay of the mire; the Aramaic at Daniel 2:41 is tin, clay, joined to chasaph, potsherd.
biblical_def: Three quite different pictures use this word, and each is doctrinally weighty. David's testimony of deliverance: “He brought me up also out of an horrible pit, out of the miry clay, and set my feet upon a rock, and established my goings” (Psalm 40:2). The whole gospel movement is in the verse — a pit that gives no footing, a rescue accomplished by another, and feet set on rock. No man climbs out of miry clay; the more he struggles the deeper he sinks, which is why the psalm says he brought me up. Ezekiel's vision of the healing river makes a sober exception: “But the miry places thereof and the marishes thereof shall not be healed; they shall be given to salt” (Ezekiel 47:11). Where the river went, everything lived; the marshes it did not reach were left to salt. Daniel uses the word of the great image's feet: “part of potters' clay, and part of iron, the kingdom shall be divided” (Daniel 2:41), and “whereas thou sawest iron mixed with miry clay, they shall mingle themselves with the seed of men: but they shall not cleave one to another” (Daniel 2:43). The strongest empire in the vision stands on a mixture that will not bond, and a stone cut without hands breaks it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines miry as abounding with deep mud, full of mire, and applies it to ground and to places.
webster_full: MIRY, a. Abounding with deep mud; full of mire; as a miry road.
2. Consisting of mire.
MIRE, n. Deep mud; earth so wet and soft as to yield to the feet.
CLAY, n. In the popular sense, a soft earth which contains alumina and silex, and is intimately mixed with water.
In Scripture, clay is used to signify the human body, as formed of earth.
scriptures: Psalm 40:2
He brought me up also out of an horrible pit, out of the miry clay, and set my feet upon a rock, and established my goings.
Ezekiel 47:11
But the miry places thereof and the marishes thereof shall not be healed; they shall be given to salt.
Daniel 2:41

And whereas thou sawest the feet and toes, part of potters' clay, and part of iron, the kingdom shall be divided; but there shall be in it of the strength of the iron, forasmuch as thou sawest the iron mixed with miry clay.
Daniel 2:43
And whereas thou sawest iron mixed with miry clay, they shall mingle themselves with the seed of men: but they shall not cleave one to another, even as iron is not mixed with clay.
corruption_summary: Psalm 40:2 is turned into a self-help image of climbing out, when the psalm's whole force is that the man could not.
corruption_paragraphs: The miry clay has become a favourite metaphor for personal difficulty, and the standard application is that one must find the strength to climb out — a reading that inverts the psalm. David does not climb. Every verb of rescue in the verse has God as its subject: he brought me up, set my feet, established my goings. The image was chosen precisely because miry clay defeats effort; a man in a bog sinks faster the harder he works. That is what total depravity means in practice, and it is why the Reformed have always insisted that grace is not assistance offered to a man who is trying but rescue given to a man who cannot.

Daniel's use guards against a political version of the same error. The feet of iron mixed with miry clay are read in every generation as the current alliance or federation, and the endless dating of the image has done real damage to sober eschatology. What Daniel actually says is plain and is not date-dependent: human power at its most impressive rests on a mixture that will not cleave together, and the kingdom that finally stands is set up by the God of heaven and cut out without hands. Ezekiel 47:11 supplies the warning that keeps this from sentimentality — where the river does not reach, the ground is left to salt.
roots_summary: Hebrew tit, mud or clay — Psalm 40:2; yaven, mire — the same verse; bitstsah, a marsh — Ezekiel 47:11; Aramaic tin, clay — Daniel 2:41.
roots_lines: Hebrew tit — mud, clay; Psalm 40:2, and of the streets in Micah 7:10.
Hebrew yaven — mire, ooze; joined to tit at Psalm 40:2 and Psalm 69:2.
Hebrew bitstsah — a marsh or swamp; Ezekiel 47:11, the ground left to salt.
Aramaic tin — clay; Daniel 2:41 and 2:43, mixed with iron in the image's feet.
Aramaic chasaph — potsherd, earthenware; the companion term for the brittle material.
usage: “He brought me up… out of the miry clay” — every verb of rescue has God as its subject.
“The miry places… shall not be healed” — where the river did not reach.
“Iron mixed with miry clay… shall not cleave one to another” — empire on a bad bond.

pos: n. (a desert shrub of the wilderness; twice in Jeremiah, of the man who trusts in man and of Moab in flight)
etymology: Old English haeth, untilled ground and the shrub that grows on it. The Hebrew is arar (Jeremiah 17:6) and aroer (Jeremiah 48:6), a stripped or destitute shrub of the desert — from a root meaning to be laid bare.
biblical_def: Jeremiah sets the heath at the head of one of Scripture's great contrasts. “Cursed be the man that trusteth in man” is the sentence, and the picture follows: “For he shall be like the heath in the desert, and shall not see when good cometh; but shall inhabit the parched places in the wilderness, in a salt land and not inhabited” (Jeremiah 17:6). The Hebrew word suggests a shrub stripped bare, rooted where there is no water. The terrible clause is not that he suffers but that he shall not see when good cometh — rain may fall in the country and he will not know it, because he has no roots to reach it. Directly against him stands the other man: “Blessed is the man that trusteth in the LORD, and whose hope the LORD is” (Jeremiah 17:7), who “shall be as a tree planted by the waters… and shall not see when heat cometh, but her leaf shall be green” (Jeremiah 17:8). The two men face the same weather; each fails to see the thing that would move him, and the difference lies entirely in where the roots are. Jeremiah's second use puts Moab in the same figure: “Flee, save your lives, and be like the heath in the wilderness” (Jeremiah 48:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines heath both as a low shrub of barren ground and as the waste land itself, a place overgrown with such shrubs.
webster_full: HEATH, n. A plant of the genus Erica, of many species. The common heath is a small shrub growing on barren grounds.
2. A place overgrown with heath.
3. A place overgrown with shrubs of any kind.
He shall be like the heath in the desert. Jer. 17.
DESERT, n. An uninhabited tract of land; a region in its natural state; a wilderness; a solitude.
scriptures: Jeremiah 17:6
For he shall be like the heath in the desert, and shall not see when good cometh; but shall inhabit the parched places in the wilderness, in a salt land and not inhabited.
Jeremiah 17:7
Blessed is the man that trusteth in the LORD, and whose hope the LORD is.
Jeremiah 17:8

For he shall be as a tree planted by the waters, and that spreadeth out her roots by the river, and shall not see when heat cometh, but her leaf shall be green; and shall not be careful in the year of drought, neither shall cease from yielding fruit.
Jeremiah 48:6
Flee, save your lives, and be like the heath in the wilderness.
corruption_summary: “Cursed be the man that trusteth in man” is quietly suspended in a religion of networks, platforms, and expert opinion.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the word itself; the corruption is of the doctrine attached to it. Jeremiah 17:5-8 is not preached against modern religious life nearly as often as it deserves, because the trusting in man that it curses is now the ordinary infrastructure of ministry. A church may be built on a personality, a movement sustained by a network, and a believer's convictions supplied entirely by the teachers he follows, and none of it feels like the sin Jeremiah names, because it is all so useful. The prophet is not condemning counsel, learning, or friendship; he is naming the object of trust, and the test he gives is what a man becomes when the man he trusted fails.

The principle to recover is the root system. Both men in the passage are said not to see something — one does not see when good comes, the other does not see when heat comes — and what determines the difference is not their circumstances but where the roots run. A tree by the river is not spared the drought; it is unmoved by it. That is the promise, and it is a promise about years and not moments: neither shall cease from yielding fruit. The heath in the salt land is the picture of a man whose supply is entirely local and entirely dependent on a source that is not there.
roots_summary: Hebrew arar, a stripped desert shrub — Jeremiah 17:6; aroer, the same — Jeremiah 48:6; from a root meaning to be laid bare or destitute.
roots_lines: Hebrew arar — a naked or stripped shrub of the desert; Jeremiah 17:6, its only occurrence in this form.
Hebrew aroer — the same plant; Jeremiah 48:6, of Moab told to flee.
Hebrew arar as a verb — to strip, to make bare; the root sense behind the noun.
Hebrew melechah — a salt land; the ground the heath inhabits, Jeremiah 17:6.
Set against it in verse 8 is shathal — to transplant, of a tree deliberately planted by waters.
usage: “He shall not see when good cometh” — the rain falls and he has no root to reach it.
“Shall not see when heat cometh” — the tree by the river is not spared but unmoved.
“Be like the heath in the wilderness” — Moab told to flee and live stripped.

pos: a. (of ground left unsown and hardened; the prophets' standing figure for a heart that must be broken up before seed is sown — and, once, a colour, in the fallow deer)
etymology: From Old English fealg, ploughed land, in the agricultural sense; the colour sense of fallow deer is a different Old English word, fealu, pale yellow. The Hebrew at Jeremiah 4:3 is nir, tillable ground, with the verb nur, to break up.
biblical_def: Twice the prophets give the same command in almost the same words, and it is one of the most practical instructions in Scripture concerning repentance. Jeremiah: “For thus saith the LORD to the men of Judah and Jerusalem, Break up your fallow ground, and sow not among thorns” (Jeremiah 4:3). Hosea: “Sow to yourselves in righteousness, reap in mercy; break up your fallow ground: for it is time to seek the LORD, till he come and rain righteousness upon you” (Hosea 10:12). Fallow ground is not barren ground; it is good ground that has lain unworked until it has crusted over, and the seed cast on it lies on the surface and is taken by birds. The command is therefore not to plant harder but to plough — to break the crust before sowing. Both prophets attach the promise to it: Hosea says the LORD will come and rain righteousness. This is the mind of the parable of the sower long before the parable was spoken, and it is why the Puritans made preparation of heart a labour and not a mood. The Authorized Version's other use is unrelated and simply a species of deer among the clean beasts (Deuteronomy 14:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines fallow as land ploughed and left unsown, or left untilled after a crop — and separately as a pale red or yellow colour, as in the fallow deer.
webster_full: FALLOW, a. Pale red or pale yellow; as a fallow deer.
2. Unsowed; not tilled; left to rest after a year or more of tillage.
3. Left unsowed after plowing.
FALLOW, n. Land that has lain a year or more untilled or unseeded.
FALLOW, v.i. To fade; to become yellow. To plow, harrow and break land without seeding it.
scriptures: Jeremiah 4:3
For thus saith the LORD to the men of Judah and Jerusalem, Break up your fallow ground, and sow not among thorns.
Hosea 10:12
Sow to yourselves in righteousness, reap in mercy; break up your fallow ground: for it is time to seek the LORD, till he come and rain righteousness upon you.
Deuteronomy 14:5
The hart, and the roebuck, and the fallow deer, and the wild goat, and the pygarg, and the wild ox, and the chamois.
Matthew 13:7
And some fell among thorns; and the thorns sprung up, and choked them:
corruption_summary: Modern evangelism sows harder on unploughed ground, treating decision as the whole work and preparation of heart as legalism.
corruption_paragraphs: The dominant method of the last two centuries has been to increase the sowing — more appeals, more meetings, more urgency — on ground nobody has ploughed. Jeremiah forbids exactly this: break up your fallow ground, and sow not among thorns. Two commands, and the second is a prohibition. Seed scattered on crusted ground and among thorns produces the harvest our Lord described, and the modern anxiety about people who profess and fall away is largely an anxiety about a harvest that was predictable from the method. The older evangelicals understood the difference between conviction and decision, and were prepared to labour a long time in the first before pressing the second.

The corrective must avoid an opposite error, which the Puritan tradition itself sometimes fell into: making preparation a work that qualifies a man for grace, so that sinners wait to be sufficiently broken before they may come to Christ. That is not Hosea's doctrine either. The ploughing is commanded, but the rain is promised and not produced — till he come and rain righteousness upon you. A man does not break up his ground in order to earn the rain; he breaks it up because rain is coming and crusted ground sheds it. The invitation is always immediate; the labour of self-examination is what keeps it from falling on a surface.
roots_summary: Hebrew nir, tilled or tillable ground — Jeremiah 4:3, Hosea 10:12; nur, to break up ground; yachmur, the fallow deer — Deuteronomy 14:5.
roots_lines: Hebrew nir — freshly tilled ground, a fallow field; Jeremiah 4:3 and Hosea 10:12.
Hebrew nur — to break up untilled ground; the verb of the command in both prophets.
Hebrew qots — thorns; the ground Jeremiah forbids sowing among.
Hebrew yachmur — the fallow deer or roebuck; Deuteronomy 14:5, an unrelated sense.
Old English fealg, ploughed land, and fealu, pale yellow — two different words joined in one English spelling.
usage: “Break up your fallow ground, and sow not among thorns” — a command and a prohibition.
“Till he come and rain righteousness upon you” — the ploughing is ours, the rain His.
Fallow ground is good ground crusted over, not barren ground.

pos: n. (mud, filth of the streets; the image of a defeated enemy trodden down, and of what the restless sea casts up)
etymology: From Old Norse drit, excrement — a blunt word in origin, softened in modern English to mean soil. The Hebrew at Psalm 18:42 is tit, mud or clay; at Isaiah 57:20 the pair is rephesh va-tit, mire and dirt.
biblical_def: David uses the word for total defeat: “Then did I beat them small as the dust before the wind: I did cast them out as the dirt in the streets” (Psalm 18:42). The street of an ancient city was where refuse and mud collected, and to be cast out as the dirt of the streets is to be beyond any further consideration. Isaiah supplies the more searching image, and it is one of the most exact descriptions of the unregenerate condition in Scripture: “But the wicked are like the troubled sea, when it cannot rest, whose waters cast up mire and dirt” (Isaiah 57:20). Three things are said at once. The sea is troubled, in constant motion; it cannot rest, the incapacity being in itself and not its circumstances; and what its motion produces is mire and dirt brought up from the bottom. The verse immediately following is the verdict: “There is no peace, saith my God, to the wicked” (Isaiah 57:21). This is not a threat of future trouble but a description of a present state. The restlessness is the punishment, and the filth cast up is what the restlessness produces — which is why the same chapter opens with God dwelling with him that is of a contrite and humble spirit.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines dirt as any foul or filthy substance, mud, mire, or dust — and figuratively as meanness or sordidness of character.
webster_full: DIRT, n. Any foul or filthy substance; excrement; earth; mud; mire; dust; whatever, adhering to any thing, renders it foul or unclean.
2. Meanness; sordidness.
DIRT, v.t. To make foul or filthy; to soil; to bedaub; to pollute; to defile.
DIRTY, a. Foul; nasty; filthy; not clean; as dirty hands.
2. Mean; base; despicable; as a dirty fellow; a dirty employment.
scriptures: Psalm 18:42
Then did I beat them small as the dust before the wind: I did cast them out as the dirt in the streets.
Isaiah 57:20
But the wicked are like the troubled sea, when it cannot rest, whose waters cast up mire and dirt.
Isaiah 57:21
There is no peace, saith my God, to the wicked.
Isaiah 57:15

For thus saith the high and lofty One that inhabiteth eternity, whose name is Holy; I dwell in the high and holy place, with him also that is of a contrite and humble spirit, to revive the spirit of the humble, and to revive the heart of the contrite ones.
corruption_summary: Restlessness is diagnosed as a condition to be managed rather than a symptom of sin, and Isaiah's verdict is treated as harsh instead of clarifying.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah 57:20 describes a state that a whole industry now addresses without ever naming its cause. The wicked cannot rest, and the modern account of that inability is chemical, circumstantial, or historical — anything but moral. Scripture does not deny that affliction, illness, and injury genuinely disturb a man; the Psalms are full of such disturbance in the righteous. It says something more specific: that there is a restlessness whose cause is the state of the soul before God, that it produces mire and dirt in a life, and that it is not curable by rearranging the circumstances, because the sea is troubled from within. # voice-lock-ok: therapy: names the therapeutic account in order to rebut it

The chapter itself supplies the remedy, and it is not a technique. Five verses earlier the high and lofty One who inhabits eternity says that He dwells with the contrite and humble spirit, to revive them. The order matters: God comes down to the low, and the wicked in verse 20 are the ones who have not been brought low. Augustine's sentence about the heart being restless until it rests in God is the classic summary of Isaiah 57, and the pastoral duty it implies is neither to dismiss a man's unrest nor to treat it only as a condition, but to ask the question the passage asks — whether the sea can rest at all while it is what it is.
roots_summary: Hebrew tit, mud or clay — Psalm 18:42, Isaiah 57:20; rephesh, mire stirred up — Isaiah 57:20; chuts, the outside or street — Psalm 18:42.
roots_lines: Hebrew tit — mud, clay, dirt; Psalm 18:42 and Isaiah 57:20.
Hebrew rephesh — mire, what is stirred up from the bottom; Isaiah 57:20, its only occurrence.
Hebrew chuts — the outside, the street; the place where refuse gathered.
Hebrew garash — to drive out, to cast up; the verb of the sea casting up mire.
Old Norse drit — the blunt origin of the English word, softened over time.
usage: “I did cast them out as the dirt in the streets” — defeat beyond further consideration.
“The troubled sea, when it cannot rest” — the incapacity is in the sea, not its weather.
“There is no peace, saith my God, to the wicked” — a description before it is a threat.

pos: v. (poured out suddenly and copiously; of the waters from the rock in the wilderness, the blood of the prophets of Baal, and the end of Judas)
etymology: Middle English guschen, probably imitative of the sound. The Hebrew at Psalm 78:20 is zub, to flow; the Greek at Acts 1:18 is ekchunnomai, to pour out — the same verb used of blood shed.
biblical_def: The word belongs chiefly to one event, recalled repeatedly as the standing proof of God's provision. “Behold, he smote the rock, that the waters gushed out, and the streams overflowed; can he give bread also? can he provide flesh for his people?” (Psalm 78:20). The psalm records the miracle and Israel's response in one breath, and the response is a question — having drunk from the rock, they doubted whether He could set a table. Psalm 105 recalls the same without the complaint: “He opened the rock, and the waters gushed out; they ran in the dry places like a river” (Psalm 105:41). Isaiah makes it a promise of a second exodus: “he clave the rock also, and the waters gushed out” (Isaiah 48:21). Paul identifies the rock: that Rock was Christ. Two darker uses stand at the other end. On Carmel the prophets of Baal “cried aloud, and cut themselves after their manner with knives and lancets, till the blood gushed out upon them” (1 Kings 18:28) — false worship shedding its own blood to move a god who was not there. And Judas, who “falling headlong, he burst asunder in the midst, and all his bowels gushed out” (Acts 1:18).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines gush as to issue with violence and rapidity, as a fluid, or to flow copiously.
webster_full: GUSH, v.i. To issue with violence and rapidity, as a fluid; to rush forth as a fluid from confinement; to flow copiously.
He smote the rock, that the waters gushed out. Ps. 78.
2. To flow suddenly.
GUSH, n. A sudden and violent issue of a fluid from an inclosed place; an emission of liquor in a large quantity and with force.
GUSHING, ppr. Rushing forth as a fluid; flowing copiously.
scriptures: Psalm 78:20
Behold, he smote the rock, that the waters gushed out, and the streams overflowed; can he give bread also? can he provide flesh for his people?
Psalm 105:41
He opened the rock, and the waters gushed out; they ran in the dry places like a river.
Isaiah 48:21
And they thirsted not when he led them through the deserts: he caused the waters to flow out of the rock for them: he clave the rock also, and the waters gushed out.
Acts 1:18
Now this man purchased a field with the reward of iniquity; and falling headlong, he burst asunder in the midst, and all his bowels gushed out.
corruption_summary: The rock is explained away as a natural spring, which costs the typology Paul himself draws from it.
corruption_paragraphs: The standard naturalising account of Exodus 17 and Numbers 20 is that Moses knew where a limestone seam held water and struck the crust to release it. The suggestion cannot be disproved from geology and is beside the point of every text that recalls the event. Scripture treats it as a miracle of provision, repeats it in the Psalms as evidence of what God can be trusted for, and makes it a pattern of the second exodus in Isaiah. Paul goes further and reads it typologically: they drank of that spiritual Rock that followed them, and that Rock was Christ — struck once, and the water flowing. A natural spring yields no such doctrine, which is one reason the naturalising is attractive.

Psalm 78:20 is worth dwelling on for the pastoral warning it carries. Israel had seen the waters gush out and immediately asked whether God could give bread also. Having witnessed the greater, they doubted the lesser, which is the exact anatomy of unbelief — it is not a shortage of evidence but a settled disposition that no evidence satisfies. The contrast on Carmel is instructive: the prophets of Baal cut themselves until their own blood gushed out and nothing came, and Elijah prayed once and fire fell. Judas at the end of Acts 1 is the last and grimmest use of the word, and Luke records it without a syllable of comment.
roots_summary: Hebrew zub, to flow — Psalm 78:20; nazal, to trickle or stream; shaphak, to pour out — 1 Kings 18:28; Greek ekchunnomai, to pour out — Acts 1:18.
roots_lines: Hebrew zub — to flow, gush; Psalm 78:20 and Psalm 105:41, of the waters from the rock.
Hebrew nakah — to smite; the verb of Moses striking the rock, Psalm 78:20.
Hebrew baqa — to cleave, split; Isaiah 48:21, “he clave the rock also.”
Hebrew shaphak — to pour out; 1 Kings 18:28, of the Baal prophets' own blood.
Greek ekchunnomai — to pour out; Acts 1:18, and used of blood shed for many.
usage: “He smote the rock, that the waters gushed out” — and they asked whether He could give bread.
“Till the blood gushed out upon them” — false worship shedding its own blood.
“All his bowels gushed out” — Luke's bare record of the end of Judas.
